char.order_knights_ru: Knights of the Order and Men of Dorpat
level.alaska_1867.fact: On December 16, 1866, a special council held by Alexander II decided to sell the colony to the United States — Britain's neighbor and rival. Envoy Eduard de Stoeckl received full powers and opened talks with Secretary of State William Seward. When the telegram with the Tsar's consent arrived, Seward would not wait for morning: the treaty was signed at the State Department at about four in the morning on March 30, 1867. The price was 7.2 million dollars in gold, about two cents an acre. It was a sale, not a '99-year lease' — that legend appeared much later. On October 18 the Russian flag was lowered in Sitka. Nobody asked the native peoples — the Tlingit, Aleuts and Yupik: one empire sold another a land they had never sold. In the US the purchase was mocked as 'Seward's Icebox' until gold was found in the Klondike and in Alaska.
level.alaska_1867.goal: Grand Duke Konstantin persuades his brother to sell Alaska, and envoy Stoeckl signs the treaty with Seward — at night, for 7.2 million dollars
level.alaska_1867.hint: The decision to sell is made in Petersburg, the signing happens in Washington. Britain is yesterday's enemy, and the '99-year lease' is a fairy tale.
level.alaska_1867.intro: 1866. Russian America — Alaska and the Aleutian Islands — belongs to the Russian-American Company: a few hundred Russians, a dwindling fur trade, and the Tlingit, who consider themselves nobody's subjects. After defeat in the Crimean War one thing is clear: the British fleet can take the colony whenever it likes. The Tsar's brother, General-Admiral Konstantin Nikolayevich, has long advised selling it — but to whom?
level.alaska_1867.source: Treaty of Cession of Russian America (Washington, March 30, 1867); journal of the Special Council of December 16, 1866
level.alaska_1867.title: Russian America
level.baptism_988.fact: Vladimir sent the emperor six thousand warriors — this, historians believe, was how the Varangian Guard began. In return Basil promised him his sister, the porphyrogenita Princess Anna, as a wife — an unheard-of honor for a 'barbarian'. When the promise was dragged out, Vladimir besieged and took Korsun — Greek Chersonesus in Crimea. Anna was sent to him, the prince was baptized, married her and returned the city 'as a bride-price'. The chronicle adds the legend of the 'choice of faiths' — Islam, Judaism, Latin Christianity and Orthodoxy — and the famous line 'Drinking is the joy of the Rus''. On his return Vladimir ordered the idols thrown into the Dnieper and the people of Kyiv baptized; the traditional date is 988. The Christianization was a long process, not a single day's event, and it became the shared heritage of Rus' — of today's Russia, Ukraine and Belarus.
level.baptism_988.goal: Prince Vladimir rescues the emperor with an army, takes Korsun when the promise is delayed — and is baptized, taking Princess Anna as his wife
level.baptism_988.hint: An emperor's sister is not given to a pagan and a raider. First the treaty, then the pressure, then the font.
level.baptism_988.intro: Around 987. Vladimir Sviatoslavich, Prince of Kyiv, has recently set up idols of Perun and other gods on a hill, yet preachers of different faiths are already coming to him. In Constantinople, Emperor Basil II is desperate: the general Bardas Phokas has risen against him. The emperor asks Rus' for help.
level.baptism_988.source: 'The Tale of Bygone Years', entries for 6494–6496 (986–988); Yahya of Antioch, 'Chronicle'
level.baptism_988.title: The Baptism of Rus'
level.batu_1240.fact: Daniel left Kyiv to the thousandman Dmitr and rode off to King Béla IV of Hungary to ask for help — in vain. The Mongols battered the walls with siege engines at the Lyadsky Gate; the last defenders took refuge in the Church of the Tithes, and its vaults collapsed. On December 6, 1240 (by other reckonings, November 19) Kyiv fell. Batu spared the wounded Dmitr 'for the sake of his courage', and, according to the Galician-Volhynian Chronicle, Dmitr advised the khan not to linger but to march on Hungary. Six years later the papal envoy Plano Carpini counted barely two hundred houses in Kyiv. The fall of Kyiv belongs to the shared history of Rus' and of today's Russia, Ukraine and Belarus; Batu's army was an army of the Mongol Empire, and his ulus would later be called the Golden Horde.
level.batu_1240.goal: The prince leaves Kyiv to the voivode Dmitr, Batu's army takes the city — and the khan spares the wounded voivode for his courage
level.batu_1240.hint: The city is held by the voivode, not the prince: Daniel is seeking help beyond the mountains. Batu did not execute the brave captive — he listened to him.
level.batu_1240.intro: Autumn 1240. Batu's Mongol army has already ravaged Ryazan, Vladimir and Chernigov. The Prince of Kyiv, Mikhail of Chernigov, has fled to Hungary, and the city has been taken by Daniel Romanovich, Prince of Galicia-Volhynia. A vast army approaches Kyiv; according to the chronicle, the townspeople could not hear one another over the creaking of carts and the bellowing of camels.
level.batu_1240.source: Hypatian (Galician-Volhynian) Chronicle, entry for 1240; John of Plano Carpini, 'History of the Mongols'
level.batu_1240.title: Batu's Kyiv
level.brest_1918.fact: On January 5, 1918, the Constituent Assembly opened in the Tauride Palace; a demonstration in its support was fired on in the streets. Toward morning the head of the guard, the sailor Zheleznyakov, told Chernov: 'The guard is tired' — and later that day the Assembly was dissolved by decree. At Brest, on February 10, Trotsky announced the formula 'neither peace nor war' and left. On February 18 the Germans launched an offensive and advanced toward Petrograd almost unopposed. Lenin threatened to resign, and the Central Committee accepted the terms by a majority vote, with Trotsky abstaining. On March 3, 1918, the peace was signed: Russia lost Poland and the Baltic lands, withdrew its troops from Finland and Ukraine and recognized the Ukrainian People's Republic — about a quarter of its population and most of its coal and metal. The Left SRs left the government in protest. Lenin himself called the treaty an 'obscene peace'. After Germany's defeat in November 1918 it was annulled.
level.brest_1918.goal: The Bolsheviks disperse the Constituent Assembly, Trotsky breaks off the talks — and after the German offensive Lenin signs the Treaty of Brest
level.brest_1918.hint: You can't disperse a power you have recognized. Peace is signed only after the German blow — and only while the commissar isn't calling for war.
level.brest_1918.intro: January 1918. The elections to the Constituent Assembly — the first universal elections in the country's history — were won by the Socialist Revolutionaries; the Bolsheviks received about a quarter of the vote. The SR leader Viktor Chernov has been elected chairman of the Assembly. Meanwhile in Brest-Litovsk, Trotsky's Soviet delegation is negotiating with Germany: General Max Hoffmann demands Poland, the Baltic lands and Ukraine. The army is melting away; there is nothing to fight with.
level.brest_1918.source: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 3, 1918); V. I. Lenin, 'On the Revolutionary Phrase' (1918)
level.brest_1918.title: The Constituent Assembly and Brest
level.dark_war_1446.fact: According to the chronicle, the groom's mother, Sophia of Lithuania, tore the belt off the Squint, declaring that it had once vanished from the Moscow treasury. The brothers left, and a twenty-year war began. Yury twice occupied Moscow and died in 1434; the Squint carried on the fight, was defeated in 1436, taken prisoner and blinded. In February 1446 Shemyaka seized Vasily II at the Trinity-Sergius Monastery and blinded him 'in revenge' for his brother — from then on the prince was called the Blind (Tyomny, 'the Dark'). But the boyars, servitors and clergy, including Bishop Iona of Ryazan, backed the blind prince, and in 1447 he returned to Moscow. Shemyaka fled to Novgorod and died there in 1453 — of poison, it was said. Thus succession from father to son triumphed in the house of Moscow — at the cost of a brutal civil war.
level.dark_war_1446.goal: A scandal over a golden belt ignites war in the house of Moscow: a blinded cousin, a blinded grand prince — and the return of the Blind to the throne
level.dark_war_1446.hint: Blood for blood: Shemyaka avenges his brother. An executed rebel blinds no one, and a prince who retires to his appanage will not come back as 'the Blind'.
level.dark_war_1446.intro: 1433. After the death of Vasily I, his young son Vasily II rules in Moscow, but his uncle Yury of Zvenigorod believes that by the old order the throne should pass to him as the eldest of the family. Yury's sons — Vasily, nicknamed the Squint, and Dmitry Shemyaka — come to the grand prince's wedding. The Squint is wearing a costly golden belt.
level.dark_war_1446.source: Sophia First and Yermolin Chronicles; Moscow chronicle compilation of the late 15th century
level.dark_war_1446.title: The Dark War
level.duma_1906.fact: On July 8, 1906, Nicholas II dissolved the Duma after 72 days of work and appointed Pyotr Stolypin prime minister. About two hundred deputies gathered in Vyborg and called on the people not to pay taxes — they were later convicted and stripped of the right to stand for election. Stolypin acted 'with two hands'. After a bomb at his dacha killed dozens of people, he introduced field courts-martial: in eight months more than a thousand people were sentenced to death, and the noose was nicknamed 'Stolypin's necktie' (as the Kadet Fyodor Rodichev put it in the Duma in 1907). The decree of November 9, 1906, allowed peasants to leave the commune and take their land as private property — by 1916 about a quarter of households had done so. The Second Duma was dissolved on June 3, 1907, and the electoral law was changed in favor of the landowners. 'You want great upheavals; we want a great Russia,' Stolypin said. In 1911 he was shot at the Kyiv Opera House.
level.duma_1906.goal: Nicholas II dissolves the First Duma, Stolypin becomes prime minister — and with one hand introduces field courts-martial, while with the other he lets peasants leave the commune
level.duma_1906.hint: The Tsar never granted a ministry responsible to the Duma. The prime minister works with two hands — and both are needed.
level.duma_1906.intro: April 1906. The first State Duma in Russian history opens. The most seats belong to the Kadets — the liberals of Professor Pavel Milyukov — and to the peasant deputies of the Trudoviks. The Duma demands an amnesty, a government responsible to it, and the division of landowners' estates. The Tsar and the court see it as rebellion. Across the country manor houses are still being burned and the SR terror goes on: dozens of officials and policemen are killed every month.
level.duma_1906.source: Decree of November 9, 1906; speeches of P. A. Stolypin in the State Duma (1906–1911)
level.duma_1906.title: Stolypin's Knot
level.ekaterinburg_1918.fact: On the night of July 16–17, 1918, Commandant Yakov Yurovsky woke the prisoners on the pretext of a move and led them to the cellar. Eleven people were shot there: Nicholas II, Alexandra Feodorovna, their children Olga, Tatiana, Maria, Anastasia and Alexei, the court physician Yevgeny Botkin, the cook Ivan Kharitonov, the valet Alexei Trupp and the maid Anna Demidova. The decision was taken by the Ural Regional Soviet; historians argue over whether it had been agreed in advance with Lenin and Sverdlov or approved by Moscow after the fact. The bodies were secretly destroyed and buried. Eight days later the Whites took Yekaterinburg; investigator Nikolai Sokolov gathered the case materials. The remains were found in 1979 and confirmed by genetic testing in the 1990s and 2000s. In 2000 the Russian Orthodox Church canonized the family. Neither 'historical necessity' nor anything else makes the killing of children and servants without trial lawful.
level.ekaterinburg_1918.goal: The former tsar and his family are held in the Ipatiev House; as the Whites approach the city, the Ural Soviet decides to kill them — and on the night of July 17 they are all shot in the cellar
level.ekaterinburg_1918.hint: The open trial never took place, and they were never taken to Moscow. The decision was made in secret — and who exactly made it is still debated.
level.ekaterinburg_1918.intro: Spring 1918. The former emperor Nicholas Romanov, his wife Alexandra Feodorovna, their children — Olga, Tatiana, Maria, Anastasia and Alexei, who suffers from hemophilia — and several servants have been moved from Tobolsk to Yekaterinburg, to the house of the engineer Ipatiev, the 'House of Special Purpose'. In Moscow, Yakov Sverdlov, chairman of the Central Executive Committee, and Trotsky talk of an open trial of the former tsar. But in summer the Czechoslovak Legion and the White armies approach the city from the east.
level.ekaterinburg_1918.source: 'The Yurovsky Note' (1920); N. A. Sokolov, 'The Murder of the Imperial Family' (1925)
level.ekaterinburg_1918.title: Yekaterinburg
level.elena_1535.fact: Elena would not share power. In 1534 her uncle Mikhail Glinsky, who reproached his niece over her favorite, Prince Ivan Ovchina-Telepnev-Obolensky, was thrown into a dungeon, where he died. In 1535 Elena's government carried out a monetary reform: old coins were withdrawn, identical ones were minted across the country, and the Novgorod 'denga' bore a horseman with a spear (kopyo) — and so the 'kopeck' was born. The regent also built fortresses and the wall of Kitai-gorod. In April 1538, not yet thirty, Elena died suddenly; contemporaries already spoke of poisoning, and a study of her remains in the late 20th century found high levels of mercury — though this is not considered proof of murder. The Shuiskys seized power, and Ivan IV later remembered boyar rule as a time of humiliation. The Terrible's childhood does not explain his whole reign — but the kopeck outlived both him and the Russian Empire.
level.elena_1535.goal: The widow of Vasily III rules alone for her three-year-old son and introduces a single coin across the country — and after her sudden death the Shuisky boyars seize power
level.elena_1535.hint: Reform is carried out by the one who rules alone, not by a boyar council. The regent's death is the end of her work, not its beginning.
level.elena_1535.intro: 1533. Grand Prince Vasily III is dying; the heir, Ivan, is three years old. Power passes to his mother — young Elena Glinskaya of a Lithuanian princely family. By the will, guardians stand beside her: her uncle Mikhail Glinsky and leading boyars. The country's money is in disarray: Moscow, Novgorod and Pskov have their own coins, silver is clipped and counterfeited, prices leap.
level.elena_1535.source: 'Chronicle of the Beginning of the Tsardom'; Ivan IV, First Epistle to Andrei Kurbsky (1564)
level.elena_1535.title: Elena's Kopeck
level.geok_tepe_1881.fact: Skobelev did not hurry: the Trans-Caspian Railway began to stretch out from the Caspian, and artillery and supplies were brought up along it and on thousands of camels. The siege lasted three weeks. On January 12 (24), 1881, sappers exploded a mine under the wall, and the columns burst through the breach. Those fleeing — warriors and civilians alike — were pursued by the cavalry for several versts; the number of Teke dead is disputed, usually given as tens of thousands over the whole campaign and some eight thousand on the day of the assault and pursuit. In Turkmenistan January 12 is marked as a Day of Remembrance. Tykma Serdar eventually chose negotiation, accepted Russian allegiance and even traveled to Petersburg. In 1884 Merv submitted without a fight. The conquest of Central Asia was no 'voluntary union': the khanates, emirates and Turkmen communities had their own rulers and a choice — to resist, to bargain, or to yield to force. Colonel Nikolai Grodekov, the campaign's chief of staff, described it in four volumes.
level.geok_tepe_1881.goal: Skobelev brings up artillery by rail and blows up the wall of the Teke fortress of Geok Tepe — and soon its defender Tykma Serdar accepts Russian allegiance
level.geok_tepe_1881.hint: This fortress has already been stormed on the march — and the attack fell back. You can't come to terms with someone killed in the pursuit.
level.geok_tepe_1881.intro: 1880, the Trans-Caspian steppe. The Teke Turkmen of the Akhal-Teke oasis submit to neither Persia, nor Khiva, nor Russia. A year ago General Lomakin's Russian column tried to take their mud-brick fortress of Geok Tepe on the march — and was thrown back. Now Petersburg sends General Mikhail Skobelev. The fortress is held by tens of thousands of people — warriors and their families — and the defense is led by Tykma Serdar.
level.geok_tepe_1881.source: N. I. Grodekov, 'The War in Turkmenia. Skobelev's Campaign of 1880–1881' (1883–1884)
level.geok_tepe_1881.title: Geok Tepe
level.georgia_1801.fact: George XII asked Emperor Paul to take the kingdom under his rule but to keep the throne for his dynasty. He died in December 1800, and in January 1801 Paul signed a manifesto of annexation. After Paul's murder Alexander I hesitated: some dignitaries in the State Council proposed keeping a protectorate. But on September 12, 1801, a new manifesto abolished the Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti, and Russian officials took over its administration. Members of the house of Bagrationi, including Queen Darejan, were gradually removed to Russia; in 1803 George's widow, Queen Mariam, stabbed General Lazarev to death when he came to deport her. General Pavel Tsitsianov, himself of a Georgian family, became commander-in-chief and pressed on with conquests in the Caucasus. For part of the Georgian nobility Russia was a shield against Persia; for others it meant the loss of their own state. In 1810 the western Georgian Kingdom of Imereti was annexed as well.
level.georgia_1801.goal: The King of Kartli-Kakheti asks Russia for protection while keeping his dynasty, but after his death Petersburg abolishes the kingdom and takes the Bagrationi away
level.georgia_1801.hint: Protection is requested while the king is alive. The heirs' dispute gives Petersburg a pretext. Keeping the Bagrationi means not abolishing the kingdom.
level.georgia_1801.intro: 1800. The Georgian kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti is squeezed between Persia and the Ottoman Empire. Under the Treaty of Georgievsk of 1783 it is under Russia's protection — but in 1795, when Agha Mohammad Shah sacked Tbilisi, Russian help never came. The ailing King George XII seeks a closer union with Petersburg, while his stepmother Darejan, widow of King Heraclius II, wants to pass the throne to her own sons.
level.georgia_1801.source: Treaty of Georgievsk (1783); Manifesto of Alexander I on Georgia (September 12, 1801)
level.georgia_1801.title: The Georgian Throne
level.ice_1242.fact: Alexander took the fortress of Koporye, and in March 1242, with his brother Andrey and the Suzdal regiments, he freed Pskov. On April 5, 1242, on the ice of Lake Peipus, the knights' wedge — the 'boar's head' — broke through the line but got bogged down, and the Rus' cavalry struck from the flanks; the fleeing were chased for seven versts. The Novgorod chronicle speaks of 400 (in another copy, 500) 'Germans' killed and 50 captured; the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle, of 20 knight-brothers killed and 6 taken prisoner (each knight had many servants and allied Chud warriors). The image of knights sinking beneath the ice was made famous by Eisenstein's 1938 film — it is not in the sources. That same summer the Order made peace, renounced the lands it had seized, and prisoners were exchanged. Alexander was later venerated as a saint, and his 'Life' turned the battle into a symbol.
level.ice_1242.goal: Alexander and his brother Andrey defeat the knights of the Order on the ice of Lake Peipus — and the Order gives up the lands it seized
level.ice_1242.hint: The Novgorod druzhina alone is not enough — the brother with the Suzdal regiments is needed. And knights who drowned in open water won't turn up for a prisoner exchange.
level.ice_1242.intro: 1240–1242. While Rus' lies ravaged by the Mongols, the Livonian Order and Bishop Hermann of Dorpat take Izborsk and Pskov — the Pskov boyar Tverdilo opens the gates to them. Novgorod, which had quarreled with Prince Alexander, calls him back: the Order's detachments are robbing merchants thirty versts from the city.
level.ice_1242.source: Novgorod First Chronicle, entry for 1242; the Livonian 'Rhymed Chronicle'; 'The Life of Alexander Nevsky'
level.ice_1242.title: The Ice of Lake Peipus
level.igor_1185.fact: According to the chronicle, Igor said: 'No one knows the mystery of God' — and pressed on. On the first day the Seversk regiments routed the Cuman vanguard and took their tent camps with their spoils, but by morning they were surrounded by the main forces of Khans Konchak and Gza. The battle by the Kayala River lasted three days; Igor, Vsevolod and their sons were captured, and almost the whole army perished. The Cumans then struck at Pereyaslavl and the Posemye lands. Konchak kept Igor in honorable captivity — he gave his daughter in marriage to Igor's son Vladimir. Igor escaped with the help of the baptized Cuman Ovlur (Lavr in the chronicle). From these events grew 'The Tale of Igor's Campaign' — a work in which Yaroslavna's lament at Putivl became a famous poetic image; the 'Tale' itself poeticizes a great deal, and scholars long debated its authenticity.
level.igor_1185.goal: Prince Igor of Novgorod-Seversky rides into the steppe without allies, is captured by Khan Konchak — and escapes back to Rus'
level.igor_1185.hint: Only someone who has been captured can escape — and the one who gets captured is the one who did not turn back. Tears alone won't free a prisoner.
level.igor_1185.intro: Spring 1185. A year ago Sviatoslav, Prince of Kyiv, and other princes defeated the Cumans, but Igor Sviatoslavich, Prince of Seversk, took no part in that campaign. Now he wants glory for himself: with his brother Vsevolod, his son and his nephew, he rides out into the steppe. On the way, by the Donets, an eclipse covers the sun — an evil omen.
level.igor_1185.source: Hypatian Chronicle, entry for 1185; 'The Tale of Igor's Campaign'
level.igor_1185.title: The Captivity of Prince Igor
level.ilya_muromets.fact: The bylina tells how wandering pilgrims came to Ilya and asked for a drink; he rose, handed them a cup and drank himself — and felt a great strength within him. Ilya rode to Kyiv by the straight road, routed an enemy army near Chernigov, and by the Smorodina River shot out Nightingale's right eye with an arrow and tied him to his stirrup. At Prince Vladimir's feast no one believed the hero: 'The country bumpkin is lying.' Then Ilya brought out his captive, and the prince asked Nightingale to whistle 'at half-strength' — he whistled with all his might, the palace shook, and the bogatyrs fell down. Ilya took Nightingale out into the open field and cut off his head. The Kyiv of the byliny is no reconstruction of the 10th century: these songs were recorded in the 18th–19th centuries in the Russian North, and Prince Vladimir in them is a composite figure. The relics of Ilya of Murom have been venerated in the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra since the 17th century, but the link between that man and the hero of the byliny cannot be proven.
level.ilya_muromets.goal: Healed after years of lying helpless, the hero Ilya rides to Kyiv by the straight road, captures Nightingale the Robber and proves to the prince that he is not lying
level.ilya_muromets.hint: A man who cannot stand won't gallop until someone raises him. Without a captive, a tale of the straight road told at the feast will sound like boasting.
level.ilya_muromets.intro: The village of Karacharovo near Murom. For thirty-three years the peasant's son Ilya has been unable to rise from the stove. The straight road from Chernigov to Kyiv has grown over: Nightingale the Robber sits in seven oaks, and his whistle flattens forests and kills people. In Kyiv, 'Fair Sun' Prince Vladimir feasts with his bogatyrs.
level.ilya_muromets.source: The bylina 'Ilya Muromets and Nightingale the Robber' as recorded by P. N. Rybnikov (1861–1867) and A. F. Hilferding (1871)
level.ilya_muromets.title: Ilya Muromets and Nightingale the Robber
level.kalka_1223.fact: The princes decided to meet the enemy in the steppe. The Mongol envoys, who proposed that they stay out of it, were killed. On May 31, 1223, on the Kalka River, Mstislav the Bold with the Cumans and the Volhynians attacked first without warning the Prince of Kyiv, Mstislav Romanovich. The Cumans broke and, as they fled, trampled the Rus' regiments. The Prince of Kyiv held a fortified camp on a hill for three days until Ploskinya, leader of the brodniki, kissed the cross that the prisoners would be released for ransom. The princes were handed over; according to the Novgorod First Chronicle, they were crushed under boards on which the victors feasted. At least nine princes died, and, according to the chronicle, only one warrior in ten came home. The Mongols reached the Dnieper and turned back — it was a reconnaissance campaign, not a conquest; fourteen years later they returned with Batu.
level.kalka_1223.goal: The princes of Rus' march to help the Cumans, but at the Kalka they fight separately — and Subutai's Mongol force beats them one by one
level.kalka_1223.hint: The Mongols won not by numbers but by the princes' disunity: one prince attacked without waiting for another. Unified command would no longer be the history of 1223.
level.kalka_1223.intro: 1223. From beyond the Caucasus an army never seen before emerges into the Cuman steppes — the Mongol corps of the generals Jebe and Subutai. The defeated Cuman Khan Köten flees to his son-in-law, Mstislav the Bold, Prince of Galicia, with gifts and these words: 'Today they have taken our land, and tomorrow they will come and take yours.' The princes of southern Rus' gather in Kyiv.
level.kalka_1223.source: Novgorod First Chronicle, entry for 1224; Hypatian Chronicle; Rashid al-Din, 'Compendium of Chronicles'
level.kalka_1223.title: The Kalka
level.khodynka_1896.fact: At dawn on May 18 (30), 1896, a rumor swept through the crowd that there would not be enough gifts for everyone. People surged toward the stalls, those behind crushed those in front, and hundreds fell into the ditches and wells. According to the final official figures, 1,389 people died and more than a thousand more were injured. There were a few hundred police on the field for half a million people. Gilyarovsky got out of the crush and wrote a report in 'Russkiye Vedomosti' that all of Russia read. The festivities were not canceled, and in the evening the emperor and empress went to a ball given by the French ambassador Montebello: relatives convinced them that an ally must not be offended. The Tsar gave a thousand rubles to each family of the dead, and his uncle was nicknamed 'Prince Khodynsky'; the nickname 'Bloody' stuck to Nicholas later, after January 9, 1905. The Moscow chief of police was officially named as the culprit. Khodynka was not a 'curse on the reign' — it was a failure of organization and responsibility.
level.khodynka_1896.goal: At the coronation festivities Khodynka Field turns into a crush in which more than a thousand people die — and in the evening Nicholas II goes to the ball anyway
level.khodynka_1896.hint: Disaster strikes where things were poorly prepared. Mourning would be fitting, but there was none that evening.
level.khodynka_1896.intro: May 1896, Moscow. Nicholas II and Alexandra Feodorovna have just been crowned in the Dormition Cathedral. The Governor-General of Moscow, Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich, the Tsar's uncle, is preparing a people's festival on Khodynka Field — a training ground scarred with ditches and old wells. Everyone has been promised a gift from the Tsar: an enamel mug with the monogram, a gingerbread, a sausage. Hundreds of thousands gather on the field from the night before. Among them is the reporter Vladimir Gilyarovsky.
level.khodynka_1896.source: Diary of Nicholas II (May 18, 1896); V. A. Gilyarovsky, report in 'Russkiye Vedomosti' (May 1896)
level.khodynka_1896.title: Khodynka
level.khovanshchina_1682.fact: On May 15, 1682, a rumor was spread through Moscow that the Naryshkins had strangled Tsarevich Ivan. The streltsy burst into the Kremlin. Tsaritsa Natalya Kirillovna led the living Ivan and Peter out onto the Red Staircase, but it no longer helped: for three days the streltsy killed boyars, among them Artamon Matveyev and the Tsaritsa's brothers — before the eyes of nine-year-old Peter. At the streltsy's demand both brothers were crowned tsars — a double throne was made for them with a little window at the back through which they were prompted — and Sophia became regent. In the summer Khovansky, who was close to the Old Believers, staged a debate on the faith in the Palace of Facets and behaved like the master of Moscow. The court left the capital, Sophia summoned Khovansky and his son to the village of Vozdvizhenskoye, and on September 17 they were executed without trial. The streltsy submitted. Sophia ruled for seven years until Peter removed her in 1689; the streltsy revolt of 1698 was the last.
level.khovanshchina_1682.goal: A streltsy revolt puts two tsars on the throne at once, Ivan and Peter, Tsarevna Sophia becomes regent — and she is the one who executes the streltsy leader Khovansky
level.khovanshchina_1682.hint: A living tsarevich on the staircase quells the revolt Sophia needs. One tsar means victory for the Naryshkins. And the streltsy leader is executed by someone other than the streltsy.
level.khovanshchina_1682.intro: April 1682. The childless Tsar Fyodor Alexeyevich has died. He has two brothers by different mothers: the sickly fifteen-year-old Ivan of the Miloslavsky clan and the lively nine-year-old Peter of the Naryshkin clan. The boyars have proclaimed Peter tsar. Their sister, the clever and ambitious Tsarevna Sophia, will not give way. The Moscow streltsy are embittered by delayed pay and by abuses from their colonels, and Prince Ivan Khovansky will soon head their Streltsy Office.
level.khovanshchina_1682.source: Sylvester Medvedev, 'A Brief Contemplation of the Years 7190, 91 and 92'; Andrei Matveyev, 'Notes'
level.khovanshchina_1682.title: Khovanshchina
level.kulikovo_1380.fact: On the night before September 8, 1380, the Rus' regiments crossed the Don and took up position on Kulikovo Field where the Nepryadva flows into it. After the duel between the hero Peresvet and the Horde champion Chelubey (known from the 'Tale'), the slaughter began; the Horde broke through the left flank, but the ambush regiment of Vladimir of Serpukhov and the voivode Bobrok struck them in the rear. Mamai fled, and Jogaila arrived too late. The victory was enormous as a symbol but did not free Rus': two years later Khan Tokhtamysh burned Moscow, and tribute was paid for another hundred years. The blessing of Sergius of Radonezh is known from the later 'Tale of the Rout of Mamai' — historians argue whether it belongs to this battle. The nickname 'Donskoy' attached itself to Dmitry later. Mamai himself was defeated by Tokhtamysh and died in Kaffa.
level.kulikovo_1380.goal: Prince Dmitry crosses the Don and meets Mamai's army on Kulikovo Field — the outcome is decided by the ambush regiment
level.kulikovo_1380.hint: You can sit it out beyond the Oka, but then there will be no battle. An ambush is not thrown into battle first — it waits until the enemy turns his back.
level.kulikovo_1380.intro: 1380. The Horde is in turmoil — the 'Great Troubles': khans replace one another in quick succession. The western part of the Horde is ruled by Mamai. He is not a khan but a beklarbek — a warlord who puts his own puppets on the throne — and he demands tribute from Moscow as before. Prince Dmitry Ivanovich of Moscow gathers the regiments of the princes of North-Eastern Rus'. The Lithuanian prince Jogaila is marching to help Mamai.
level.kulikovo_1380.source: 'Zadonshchina'; 'The Tale of the Rout of Mamai'; the chronicle tale of the Battle of Kulikovo (Rogozhsky Chronicler)
level.kulikovo_1380.title: Kulikovo Field
level.kyiv_882.fact: 'The Tale of Bygone Years' says that Oleg hid his warriors in the boats and sent word to Askold and Dir that merchants had come. When they came out, he brought forward Igor: 'You are not princes nor of princely blood, but I am of princely blood, and this is Rurik's son' — and they were killed; Oleg settled in Kyiv and said: 'Let this be the mother of Rus' cities.' The details are chronicle legend: the dates in the early part of the 'Tale' were calculated after the fact, and Askold and Dir may have ruled at different times. What matters is something else: this is how a realm centered on the Dnieper took shape, on the route 'from the Varangians to the Greeks'. Early Rus', with centers in Kyiv, Novgorod and other lands, is the shared heritage of several modern peoples, not the history of any single present-day state.
level.kyiv_882.goal: Posing as a merchant, Oleg lures the rulers of Kyiv onto the riverbank and, showing them the young Igor, takes Kyiv
level.kyiv_882.hint: The hills of Kyiv can't be taken head-on. Cunning comes first, and the child grants the right to rule only to someone already on the bank.
level.kyiv_882.intro: Around 882. After Rurik's death his kinsman Oleg rules in the north as guardian of Rurik's little son Igor. With an army of Varangians, Slovenes, Krivichs and Chud, Oleg sails down the Dnieper. In Kyiv, on the high bank, sit Askold and Dir — Varangians who once left Rurik and took power over the Polianians.
level.kyiv_882.source: 'The Tale of Bygone Years', entry for 6390 (882)
level.kyiv_882.title: The Throne of Kyiv
level.kyiv_sack_1169.fact: In 1169 Andrey assembled an army of eleven princes led by his son Mstislav. On March 8 Kyiv was taken and, in the chronicler's words, 'the whole city' was plundered for two days — Podil, the Hill, the monasteries and St. Sophia's Cathedral; Mstislav Izyaslavich fled to Volhynia. For the first time the throne of Kyiv was taken in such a way that the victor did not sit on it: Andrey gave Kyiv to his younger brother Gleb and stayed in Vladimir himself. The center of power was shifting, and seniority was separating from Kyiv itself. This was not 'Russia attacking Ukraine' — no such states existed yet: it was a struggle between princely lines of one dynasty within fragmented Rus'. Andrey himself was murdered by his own boyars at Bogolyubovo in 1174.
level.kyiv_sack_1169.goal: Andrey Bogolyubsky takes Kyiv with eleven princes but does not take its throne himself — seniority moves to wherever the prince is
level.kyiv_sack_1169.hint: One prince alone can't handle Kyiv — allies are needed. The key to this campaign is where the prince does not go.
level.kyiv_sack_1169.intro: The 1160s. Rus' is split into principalities, but the throne of Kyiv is still considered the senior one, and different branches of the Rurikids fight over it. In the north-east, in the land of Vladimir-Suzdal, rules Andrey, son of Yury Dolgoruky. He is building white-stone Vladimir and his residence at Bogolyubovo. In Kyiv sits his rival Mstislav Izyaslavich of the Volhynian branch.
level.kyiv_sack_1169.source: Kyiv Chronicle within the Hypatian Chronicle, entry for 1169; Laurentian Chronicle, 1169
level.kyiv_sack_1169.title: The Sack of Kyiv
level.lyubech_1097.fact: In 1096 Monomakh wrote Oleg a letter preserved in the chronicle: he forgave the death of his son and called for peace. In 1097 the princes gathered at Liubech and resolved: 'Let each hold his own patrimony' — and kissed the cross on it. This was a new principle: lands were fixed to branches of the dynasty instead of passing along the ladder of seniority. But soon after the council, Davyd Igorevich, Prince of Volhynia, convinced Grand Prince Sviatopolk that Vasilko, Prince of Terebovl, was plotting against them — Vasilko was seized and blinded. A new war began. The council did not stop fragmentation; if anything, it formalized it. Monomakh would later rally the princes against the Cumans and in 1113 became Prince of Kyiv. His 'Instruction' to his children is one of the first texts about what a ruler should be.
level.lyubech_1097.goal: The princes gather at Liubech and swear that 'each shall hold his patrimony' — and a few days later they blind one of their own
level.lyubech_1097.hint: There will be no peace while the chief troublemaker is beaten rather than reconciled. And an oath by itself does not protect against slander.
level.lyubech_1097.intro: The late 11th century. The descendants of Yaroslav the Wise divide Rus' and fight one another; Oleg Sviatoslavich brings the Cumans into Rus', for which he will be nicknamed Gorislavich, 'son of sorrow'. The Cumans burn villages while the princes are busy with their feuds. Vladimir Monomakh, Prince of Pereyaslavl, who has himself lost a son in the war with Oleg, wants to stop the war of all against all.
level.lyubech_1097.source: 'The Tale of Bygone Years', entries for 6604–6605 (1096–1097) (Monomakh's letter to Oleg, the priest Vasily's account of Vasilko's blinding); 'The Instruction of Vladimir Monomakh'
level.lyubech_1097.title: The Council of Liubech
level.metropolitan_1448.fact: Grand Prince Vasily II declared Isidore an apostate and ordered him confined in the Chudov Monastery; in the autumn of 1441 he escaped — through Tver and Lithuania to Rome. Vasily wrote to Constantinople asking for a new metropolitan to be installed, but the emperor and the patriarchate held to the union. In 1448 a council of Rus' bishops elected Bishop Iona of Ryazan metropolitan on its own — for the first time without Constantinople's sanction. In 1451–1452 Moscow explained this in a letter to Emperor Constantine XI. A year later Constantinople fell. Thus the Rus' metropolitanate became autocephalous in fact, though this was formally recognized later; the formula 'Moscow, the Third Rome' appeared only in the early 16th century, with the Pskov monk Philotheus. In the lands of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania a separate Metropolitanate of Kyiv soon emerged.
level.metropolitan_1448.goal: Moscow rejects the Union of Florence, the Greek metropolitan flees to Rome — and for the first time the Rus' bishops install a metropolitan themselves
level.metropolitan_1448.hint: The union is the whole question: accepting it defeats the purpose of the council. And don't wait for a metropolitan from Constantinople — it now stands for the union.
level.metropolitan_1448.intro: 1441. Isidore, the Greek Metropolitan of Kyiv and All Rus', returns to Moscow from Italy. At the council in Florence the Church of Constantinople, hoping for Western help against the Turks, signed a union with Rome, and Isidore became a cardinal. In the Dormition Cathedral he commemorates the Pope and reads out the charter on the union of the churches.
level.metropolitan_1448.source: Simeon of Suzdal, 'The Tale of the Eighth Council'; letter of Vasily II to Emperor Constantine (c. 1451)
level.metropolitan_1448.title: A Metropolitan Without Constantinople
level.nerchinsk_1689.fact: Neither the Russians nor the Manchus knew each other's languages, so the talks were held in Latin: on the Qing side the Jesuits Jean-François Gerbillon and Thomas Pereira interpreted, on the Russian side the translator Andrei Belobotsky. Kangxi ordered his envoys to demand the whole Amur but allowed them to cede Nerchinsk if necessary. The talks lasted two weeks and more than once came to the brink of war: Qing troops surrounded the town. Golovin understood that fighting such forces was impossible. On August 27, 1689, the treaty was signed: the border ran along the Argun River and over the mountains to the Sea of Okhotsk, Albazin was razed, the Amur basin remained with the Qing, but the merchants of both countries gained the right to trade. The text was drawn up in Latin, Russian and Manchu. It was Russia's first treaty with China, and it lasted almost 170 years — until the Treaty of Aigun in 1858.
level.nerchinsk_1689.goal: The Russian and Qing envoys negotiate in Latin through Jesuits: Russia gives up the Amur and in return gains peace and trade with China
level.nerchinsk_1689.hint: The envoys speak in the emperor's name — his decree comes first. Without an interpreter they can't understand each other. Fighting here means losing.
level.nerchinsk_1689.intro: 1689. For forty years Russian Cossacks and trappers have been settling the Amur, home to the Daurs and Evenks, who paid tribute to the Qing Empire. The Qing army has twice besieged the Russian fort of Albazin. Now a huge embassy of the Kangxi Emperor led by Prince Songgotu has arrived under the walls of Nerchinsk — with an army several times larger than the Russian garrison. From Moscow the okolnichy Fyodor Golovin has been sent to meet it.
level.nerchinsk_1689.source: Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689); Jean-François Gerbillon, journals of his travels into Tartary (in Du Halde's 'Description of the Chinese Empire', 1735)
level.nerchinsk_1689.title: The Treaty of Nerchinsk
level.novgorod_1478.fact: Mikhail Olelkovich stayed in Novgorod only a few months. In the summer of 1471 the Muscovite army routed the Novgorodians on the Shelon River; Moscow proclaimed the campaign a war against 'Latinism', although only Casimir was a Catholic — the Novgorodians were Orthodox. By the Peace of Korostyn Novgorod acknowledged itself the grand prince's 'patrimony' but kept its institutions. In 1477 Ivan III demanded to be called 'sovereign' rather than 'lord' and besieged the city. In January 1478 Archbishop Feofil and the boyars accepted the terms: 'There shall be no veche bell, there shall be no posadnik, and we shall hold our sovereign power.' The bell was carried off to Moscow, Marfa Boretskaya was sent into exile, and hundreds of families were later resettled. Novgorod was not a modern democracy — it was run by a boyar elite — but nor was it a 'nest of treason': Moscow liquidated an independent city republic.
level.novgorod_1478.goal: Novgorod's boyar party seeks support in Lithuania, Moscow wins on the Shelon — and Ivan III takes away the veche bell
level.novgorod_1478.hint: Moscow needs a pretext — an alliance with Lithuania. And whoever swears to keep the old ways can no longer say 'there shall be no veche'.
level.novgorod_1478.intro: 1470. Lord Novgorod the Great is a rich trading republic: it is governed by the veche, the posadniks and the archbishop, while the prince is merely hired to serve. Grand Prince Ivan III of Moscow demands ever more power. The party of Marfa Boretskaya, a posadnik's widow, and her sons invites the Lithuanian prince Mikhail Olelkovich from Kyiv and seeks an alliance with King Casimir IV.
level.novgorod_1478.source: Moscow chronicle compilation of 1479; Novgorod Fourth Chronicle
level.novgorod_1478.title: The Veche Falls Silent
level.october_1917.fact: On October 10, at a secret meeting of the Bolshevik Central Committee, a vote of ten to two decided to prepare an uprising; Kamenev and Zinoviev opposed it and even wrote about it in a newspaper. The Military Revolutionary Committee of the Petrograd Soviet, in which Trotsky played the leading role, brought the garrison regiments under its control. On the night before October 25, detachments seized the bridges, stations and telegraph. In the morning Kerensky left the city to fetch troops — by car, not in a woman's dress, as legend later claimed. On the night of October 25–26 the Winter Palace was taken almost without a fight, and the ministers were arrested; the famous 'storming' looks more like footage from Eisenstein's film 'October' (1928). The Congress of Soviets adopted the decrees on peace and on land; the Mensheviks and Right SRs walked out of the congress in protest. Some call these events a revolution, others an armed coup: the term depends on the tradition. A Bolshevik victory was not inevitable.
level.october_1917.goal: Lenin wins a Central Committee decision to rise up, Trotsky takes over the garrison through the Military Revolutionary Committee — and the Provisional Government falls
level.october_1917.hint: Whoever waits for elections won't start an uprising. As long as the premier has no loyal troops, the palace can't be defended.
level.october_1917.intro: October 1917, Petrograd. Since the Tsar's abdication the country has been ruled by Alexander Kerensky's Provisional Government — but alongside it stands the Petrograd Soviet. The war goes on, landowners' estates are being seized in the countryside, and the cities lack bread. The Bolsheviks have won a majority in the Petrograd Soviet, and its chairman is Leon Trotsky. Lenin, in hiding since the July Days, demands that power be taken at once. Lev Kamenev objects: the Constituent Assembly is only a month away.
level.october_1917.source: Minutes of the Central Committee of the RSDLP(b), October 10, 1917; John Reed, 'Ten Days That Shook the World' (1919)
level.october_1917.title: October
level.oleg_horse.fact: The chronicle entry for 912 tells that the sorcerer answered that the prince would die from his beloved horse. Oleg ordered the horse led away, fed and never brought to him again. Some years later, back from a campaign against the Greeks, he asked about the horse and was told it had died. The prince laughed: 'The volkhvs speak falsely, it is all lies' — and rode out to look at its bones. Stepping on the skull, he said: 'Is it from this skull that my death will come?' — a snake crawled out of it and bit him on the foot, and of this Oleg died. A similar story appears in the Icelandic saga of Arrow-Odd, so this is a wandering motif about a fate that cannot be cheated, not a verifiable fact. Pushkin turned it into 'The Song of Oleg the Seer' (1822). The chronicles even disagree on where his grave lies: Kyiv or Ladoga.
level.oleg_horse.goal: A sorcerer foretells the prince's death from his horse, Oleg sends the horse away — and still dies from a snake in its skull
level.oleg_horse.hint: To fear the horse, he must first hear the prophecy. Whoever climbs back into the saddle will learn nothing about his fate.
level.oleg_horse.intro: The early 10th century, Kyiv. Prince Oleg is a ruler nicknamed the Seer, that is, one who knows the future. He has campaigned against Tsargrad and nailed his shield to its gates. He has a beloved warhorse. One day the prince asks the volkhvs and sorcerers what is destined to bring about his death.
level.oleg_horse.source: 'The Tale of Bygone Years', entry for 6420 (912); A. S. Pushkin, 'The Song of Oleg the Seer' (1822)
level.oleg_horse.title: Oleg the Seer and His Horse
level.olga_945.fact: According to 'The Tale of Bygone Years', the Drevlians, led by Prince Mal, reasoned: 'If the wolf takes to the sheep, he will carry off the whole flock unless he is killed' — and killed Igor near Iskorosten. Then they sent matchmakers to Olga: Mal wished to marry the widow. The chronicle describes Olga's four revenges in detail — envoys buried in their boat, others burned in a bathhouse, Drevlians slaughtered at the funeral feast, and Iskorosten burned with the help of birds carrying burning tow. These stories are heavily legendary. What is more reliable is this: afterwards Olga 'established statutes and dues' — fixed amounts of tribute — and pogosts, the places where it was collected. This is one of the first known administrative reforms in Rus': collecting tribute became more predictable and safer. Later Olga was baptized in Constantinople and ruled on behalf of her young son.
level.olga_945.goal: Prince Igor's greed costs him his life, and his widow Olga takes revenge on the Drevlians and introduces fixed tribute — 'uroki' and pogosts
level.olga_945.hint: Reform is born of disaster. Mal's courtship is not peace but surrender; and until the Drevlians are subdued, no one will accept fixed dues.
level.olga_945.intro: 945. Prince Igor, ruling in Kyiv, collects tribute from the subject tribes — this is called the poliudie. His retainers grumble: the men of the voivode Sveneld are better dressed than they are. Igor goes to the Drevlians, takes tribute — and decides to go back for a second round. His wife Olga stays in Kyiv with their little son Sviatoslav.
level.olga_945.source: 'The Tale of Bygone Years', entries for 6453–6455 (945–947); Constantine Porphyrogenitus, 'De Administrando Imperio', ch. 9 (on the poliudie)
level.olga_945.title: Olga's Fixed Dues
level.pereyaslav_1654.fact: On October 1, 1653, the Zemsky Sobor in Moscow decided to take the Zaporozhian Host 'under the high hand' of the Tsar. In January 1654 the embassy of Boyar Vasily Buturlin arrived in Pereiaslav. On January 8 the Rada of the hetman and the Cossacks agreed to pass under the Tsar's rule. But in the church there was a hitch: the Cossack officers demanded that the envoy swear in the Tsar's name to preserve the Cossack liberties, and Buturlin refused — 'the Tsar does not swear to his subjects'. The Cossacks took the oath nonetheless, and decided to secure their rights on paper. In March in Moscow their envoys received the 'March Articles': an elected hetman, their own courts, a register of 60,000 Cossacks, the right to receive foreign envoys — with reservations: embassies were to be reported to the Tsar, and there were to be no dealings with the Commonwealth or the Ottoman Empire without the Tsar's decree. The two sides understood the agreement differently: Moscow as subjecthood, the hetman and officers as an alliance under protection with broad autonomy. This was neither an 'eternal reunification' nor a modern referendum. As early as 1658 Ivan Vyhovsky, who had become hetman, concluded the Treaty of Hadiach with the Commonwealth, and decades of wars began that the Cossacks called the Ruin.
level.pereyaslav_1654.goal: The Hetmanate, at war with the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, seeks Moscow's protection: the Rada swears allegiance to the Tsar, and the Host's rights are written down in the March Articles — each side understands the agreement its own way
level.pereyaslav_1654.hint: First the request and the Assembly's decision, then the Rada. Demanding an oath from the envoy means wrecking the Rada. And rights not written down on paper are worth nothing.
level.pereyaslav_1654.intro: 1653. Bohdan Khmelnytsky's uprising against the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth is in its sixth year. The Cossack Host holds a huge part of the Dnieper lands — but its Tatar allies are unreliable and its strength is running out. The hetman is looking for a protector: he corresponds with the Turkish Sultan, with Moscow, with his neighbors. Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich long hesitates: accepting the Cossacks means war with Poland.
level.pereyaslav_1654.source: Report of V. V. Buturlin's embassy (1654); the March Articles of Bohdan Khmelnytsky (1654)
level.pereyaslav_1654.title: The Rada at Pereiaslav
level.pogroms_1882.fact: The pogroms of 1881–1882 struck some two hundred places in the Pale of Settlement; shops and homes were wrecked, and there were killings and rapes. Historians have found no proof that the government organized them, but local authorities often hesitated and troops arrived late. The official version turned everything upside down: the culprits were not the rioters but the Jews' 'exploitation' of the peasants. Ignatyev's commissions prepared the 'Temporary Regulations' of May 3, 1882: Jews were forbidden to settle anew in the countryside or to buy land there. The 'temporary' regulations lasted until 1917, and were later joined by quotas in the gymnasiums and the expulsion from Moscow in 1891. In 1882 Leon Pinsker anonymously published the pamphlet 'Auto-Emancipation' in Berlin: equality will not be handed down; the Jews need a home of their own. He went on to lead the Hovevei Zion movement. Over thirty years about two million Jews left the empire — most of them for the United States.
level.pogroms_1882.goal: After the pogroms the authorities blame not the rioters but the victims: Ignatyev pushes through the 'Temporary Regulations', and the Odesa doctor Leon Pinsker writes 'Auto-Emancipation'
level.pogroms_1882.hint: A law against the victims begins with shifting the blame onto them. Someone still waiting for mercy from above won't write an appeal.
level.pogroms_1882.intro: Spring 1881. The Narodnaya Volya revolutionaries have killed Alexander II, and rumors are creeping across the south of the empire that the Jews are to blame and that 'the Tsar has allowed it'. On April 15 a pogrom breaks out in Elisavetgrad — followed by dozens more: Kyiv, Odesa, the shtetls. The new emperor Alexander III and the Minister of the Interior, Count Nikolai Ignatyev, decide what to do. And in Odesa the doctor Leon Pinsker, who all his life believed that Jews would become equal subjects through enlightenment, looks at the wrecked houses.
level.pogroms_1882.source: 'Temporary Regulations' of May 3, 1882; Leon Pinsker, 'Auto-Emancipation' (1882); I. Michael Aronson, 'Troubled Waters' (1990)
level.pogroms_1882.title: The May Laws
level.poltava.fact: On June 27, 1709, Peter I's army routed Charles XII's Swedes near Poltava. The Cossack officers were split: some backed Mazepa, others Peter; after the defeat Mazepa fled with Charles to Bender. The victory turned the tide of the Northern War and made Russia a great European power.
level.poltava.hint: Let Peter first assemble and drill a regular army — only an army that is ready will defeat the Swede Charles at Poltava. Mazepa is not the target.
level.poltava.intro: Charles XII has invaded Russia, and Hetman Mazepa has gone over to his side, hoping to preserve the autonomy of the Hetmanate, and led part of the Cossacks to the Swede. The fate of the war is being decided.
level.raskol_1666.fact: Nikon pushed the reform through harshly: dissenters were defrocked and exiled. Avvakum and his family were sent to Siberia, to Dauria, where for years he trudged along with the voivode Pashkov. But Nikon styled himself 'Great Sovereign' and quarreled with the Tsar; in 1658 he ostentatiously withdrew to his New Jerusalem Monastery. In 1664 the Tsar invited the returned Avvakum to become a corrector of books and promised him money, but the archpriest again denounced the reform and was again exiled. The Great Moscow Council of 1666–1667, attended by Patriarchs Paisius of Alexandria and Macarius of Antioch, stripped Nikon of his rank — but confirmed the new rites and anathematized the old ones. Supporters of the old rite, whom the authorities called 'schismatics', fled into the forests and abroad; in the 1670s they were suppressed by force at Solovki and elsewhere, and some communities burned themselves rather than surrender. Boyarina Feodosia Morozova was starved to death in the Borovsk prison in 1675. Avvakum, after fifteen years in an earthen pit prison at Pustozersk, was burned in 1682. He left his 'Life' — one of the first Russian autobiographies. The Old Belief lives on to this day.
level.raskol_1666.goal: Patriarch Nikon changes the rite, Archpriest Avvakum will not yield, and the Council of 1666–1667 deposes Nikon — but keeps his reform and anathematizes the old rite
level.raskol_1666.hint: It is not the loudest debater who goes on trial, but the one who quarreled with the Tsar. An archpriest who accepted the Tsar's gift would no longer be Archpriest Avvakum.
level.raskol_1666.intro: 1653. Patriarch Nikon, a friend of the young Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich, wants to bring Russian books and rites into line with Greek models: crossing oneself with three fingers instead of two, singing 'alleluia' differently, correcting the liturgical books. To many this seems a betrayal of their fathers' faith. The fiercest opponent is Archpriest Avvakum, preacher and writer.
level.raskol_1666.source: 'The Life of Archpriest Avvakum, Written by Himself' (1672–1675); acts of the Great Moscow Council of 1666–1667
level.raskol_1666.title: The Schism
level.razin_1670.fact: In the spring of 1670 Razin's army took Tsaritsyn, then Astrakhan, where the voivode was killed. The ataman sent out 'seductive letters', calling on serfs, peasants and the peoples of the Volga — Chuvash, Mari, Mordvins, Tatars — to strike at the boyars, while calling himself a defender of the 'Great Sovereign'. The uprising engulfed a vast territory, thousands died on both sides, and in captured towns the rebels massacred nobles and officials. In October, near Simbirsk, the new-order regiments of Prince Yury Baryatinsky defeated the main forces, and the wounded Razin fled to the Don. The well-to-do Don Cossacks, led by Host Ataman Kornila Yakovlev — Razin's godfather — seized him at the Kagalnik stronghold in April 1671 and handed him over to Moscow. On June 6, 1671, Razin was quartered on Bolotnaya Square. Before the execution his brother Frol cried out 'word and deed of the sovereign' — promising to reveal a hidden treasure — and lived another five years. Songs about Razin are still sung today, though 'From Beyond the Island to the Midstream' was written only in the 19th century.
level.razin_1670.goal: Ataman Stepan Razin raises the whole Volga region, but he is defeated at Simbirsk, and his own Don Cossacks hand him over to Moscow
level.razin_1670.hint: Someone who has gone off across the sea won't raise the Volga. A voivode can defeat the army, but only his own people can hand over the ataman.
level.razin_1670.intro: 1667. The Don Cossack Stepan Razin leads the golytba — poor Cossacks with no land and no share — off 'for coats': he robs merchant caravans on the Volga, then for two years ravages the Persian shores of the Caspian. He returns a rich man and a hero. In 1670 Razin proclaims a campaign 'against the boyars and voivodes'.
level.razin_1670.source: Jan Struys, 'The Perillous and Most Unhappy Voyages' (1676); 'Foreigners' Accounts of the Uprising of Stepan Razin'
level.razin_1670.title: Razin's Flood
level.revolution_1905.fact: On January 9, 1905, the Tsar was not in the Winter Palace — he was at Tsarskoye Selo. At the Narva Gate, on Palace Square and elsewhere, troops fired on the procession. According to official figures 130 people died; other estimates put it at about two hundred or more. 'Bloody Sunday' killed faith in the good Tsar. A year of revolution began: strikes, peasant unrest, the mutiny on the battleship 'Potemkin', national movements in the borderlands. In October the whole country came to a halt — a general strike, and a Soviet of Workers' Deputies appeared in Petersburg. General Dmitry Trepov ordered 'no blank volleys, spare no cartridges', but Sergei Witte convinced Nicholas II: either dictatorship or concessions. On October 17 the Tsar signed a manifesto granting freedoms and a legislative Duma, and Witte became head of the government. The manifesto did not stop the violence: Jewish pogroms swept the country right after it, and in December the Moscow uprising was crushed with artillery. In 1906 Gapon was killed by the SRs as a police agent.
level.revolution_1905.goal: The shooting of Gapon's procession shatters faith in the Tsar, a year of strikes brings the empire to its knees — and on Witte's memorandum Nicholas II signs the October Manifesto
level.revolution_1905.hint: The manifesto is no gift: without the revolution it would not exist. And dictatorship is incompatible with it.
level.revolution_1905.intro: January 1905, Petersburg. The empire is losing the war with Japan, and the Putilov Works is on strike. Father Georgy Gapon, who founded the legal 'Assembly of Russian Factory Workers', leads the workers and their families to the Winter Palace: with icons and portraits of the Tsar they carry a petition — an eight-hour working day, a Constituent Assembly, freedom of speech. 'If you will not help us, we will die here, on this square.'
level.revolution_1905.source: The workers' petition of January 9, 1905; the Manifesto of October 17, 1905; S. Yu. Witte, 'Memoirs'
level.revolution_1905.title: Bloody Sunday and the Manifesto
level.rurik_862.fact: 'The Tale of Bygone Years', compiled in Kyiv in the early 12th century, says that in 862 the tribes drove the Varangians back across the sea and stopped paying them tribute, but began to rule themselves — and 'kin rose against kin, and there was strife among them'. Then they said: 'Our land is great and rich, but there is no order in it. Come and rule and reign over us.' Three brothers came: Rurik settled in Novgorod (in other copies, Ladoga), Sineus at Beloozero, Truvor at Izborsk; two years later the brothers died, and Rurik ruled alone. This is legend, not a record: the chronicler wrote two hundred and fifty years later, the names Sineus and Truvor are sometimes interpreted as misunderstood Scandinavian words, and historians still argue over the origin of the Rus'. The story explained where the princely dynasty of the Rurikids came from, not the 'birth' of any modern state.
level.rurik_862.goal: The northern tribes drive out the Varangians, quarrel among themselves — and then invite Prince Rurik and his brothers from across the sea
level.rurik_862.hint: First freedom, then strife, and only then the invitation. A prince who comes with the sword is no longer one who was called.
level.rurik_862.intro: The mid-9th century, the north of Eastern Europe. The Ilmen Slovenes, Krivichs, Chud and Merya pay tribute to the Varangians — warriors and traders from across the Baltic. The elders decide that they can bear it no longer. Among the Varangians is a chieftain, Rurik, with his brothers Sineus and Truvor.
level.rurik_862.source: 'The Tale of Bygone Years', entry for 6370 (862)
level.rurik_862.title: The Calling of the Varangians
level.sadko.fact: The bylina tells that the lot fell on Sadko, and he was lowered into the sea on an oak plank. On the seabed the Sea Tsar ordered him to play and broke into a dance himself — above, a storm rose, and ships and people sank. Saint Nicholas of Mozhaysk appeared and told him to break the strings and pull out the pegs, and when the Tsar offered him a wife, to choose not the beauties but the last of them, the maiden Chernava. Sadko did so, fell asleep — and woke on the steep bank of the Chernava River (in other versions, the Volkhov) near Novgorod; his ships arrived there too. In his joy he built a church of Saint Nicholas. The bylina reflects trading Novgorod with its overseas routes and merchant wealth, but the characters and miracles are fairy-tale. Some scholars link the hero to the Novgorodian Sotko Sytinich, who, according to the chronicle, built a stone church in 1167.
level.sadko.goal: The Novgorod gusli player descends to the Sea Tsar, breaks his strings on the old man's advice and, choosing Chernava as his bride, returns home
level.sadko.hint: The sea can't be bought off with gold. The most beautiful bride is not the one who will bring you home.
level.sadko.intro: Novgorod the Great. The poor gusli player Sadko grew rich by a miracle: the Sea Tsar, who loved his playing, helped him win a wager against the Novgorod merchants. Now Sadko is a rich merchant himself and leads thirty ships across the sea. But on the way back the ships stop dead in the middle of the sea: the Sea Tsar demands tribute — not in gold, but a living head.
level.sadko.source: The bylina 'Sadko' as recorded in the 'Kirsha Danilov Collection' (18th century) and by P. N. Rybnikov; Novgorod First Chronicle, 1167
level.sadko.title: Sadko
level.salt_riot_1648.fact: The duty was soon abolished, but arrears for past years began to be beaten out of people. On June 1, 1648, a crowd stopped the Tsar's horse near the Kremlin with a petition, and was driven off — and Moscow rose up: boyars' houses were sacked, the city burned. The crowd killed the Duma clerk Nazary Chistoy, and the next day the Tsar handed over Pleshcheyev, who was beaten to death on Red Square. Alexei Mikhailovich, in tears, begged the people to spare Morozov and secretly sent him to the Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery, bringing him back a few months later. Riots swept dozens of towns. The frightened government convened a Zemsky Sobor, and a commission under Prince Nikita Odoyevsky drew up the Sobornoye Ulozhenie of 1649 — a code of almost a thousand articles. It abolished the 'fixed years' for good: runaway peasants could now be hunted down and returned with no time limit. Thus a revolt against a tax ended in a law that finally bound the peasants in serfdom.
level.salt_riot_1648.goal: The salt duty stirs Moscow to revolt, the young Tsar hands a judge over to the mob but saves his tutor — and the frightened government writes the Sobornoye Ulozhenie
level.salt_riot_1648.hint: The revolt begins with a tax. The Tsar will sacrifice someone — but not the man who raised him. A new law is written once the city has calmed down.
level.salt_riot_1648.intro: 1646. Tsar Alexei Mikhailovich is seventeen, and his tutor, Boyar Boris Morozov, rules for him. The treasury is empty, and instead of direct taxes Morozov devises a huge duty on salt. Salt becomes several times more expensive, fish that can't be salted rots on the Volga, and Leonty Pleshcheyev, judge of the Zemsky Office, is notorious for bribery and cruelty.
level.salt_riot_1648.source: The Sobornoye Ulozhenie of 1649; Grigory Kotoshikhin, 'On Russia in the Reign of Alexei Mikhailovich'
level.salt_riot_1648.title: The Salt Riot
level.sech_1775.fact: The Sich stood in the way of imperial policy: the Cossacks did not obey the governors, took in runaway peasants and demanded their lands back. On the advice of Grigory Potemkin, Governor-General of New Russia, it was decided to put an end to it. On June 4, 1775, the troops of General Peter Tekeli, a Serb in Russian service, returning from the Turkish war, surrounded the Sich. Kalnyshevsky and the officers surrendered without a fight to avoid bloodshed. Catherine's manifesto of August 3, 1775, declared the Sich destroyed and the very name of 'Zaporozhian Cossacks' abolished. Kalnyshevsky was confined without trial in the Solovetsky Monastery, where he spent more than 25 years; released in 1801 as a very old man, he stayed there and died in 1803. Some of the Zaporozhians left for beyond the Danube under the Sultan's rule and founded the Danubian Sich; later many Cossacks resettled in the Kuban. This was not 'restoring order' but the end of an important Cossack institution — imperial centralization.
level.sech_1775.goal: The Zaporozhians helped defeat Turkey, but the empire no longer needs them: troops surround the Sich, and the last koshovyi otaman surrenders without a fight and goes to imprisonment at Solovki
level.sech_1775.hint: While the border is close, the Cossacks are needed. The old otaman won't shed blood — nor will he leave for beyond the Danube like the others.
level.sech_1775.intro: 1774. For six years the Zaporozhian Sich — a free Cossack host beyond the Dnieper rapids with its own rada and elected otamans — has been fighting alongside the empire against Turkey. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca pushes the border to the Black Sea. The last koshovyi otaman, Petro Kalnyshevsky — an old man who has served the Cossacks for half a century — hopes for rewards. But Empress Catherine II is already handing out the steppe around the Sich to landowners and settlers, and the Zaporozhians are quarreling with the new masters over land.
level.sech_1775.source: Manifesto of Catherine II on the Destruction of the Zaporozhian Sich (August 3, 1775); Dmytro Yavornytsky, 'History of the Zaporozhian Cossacks' (1892–1897)
level.sech_1775.title: The End of the Zaporozhian Sich
level.shamil_1859.fact: For a quarter of a century Shamil fought a huge army, and punitive expeditions only multiplied his supporters. There were conflicts within the imamate too: in 1851 the famous naib Hadji Murad quarreled with the imam and went over to the Russians, and half a year later was killed trying to escape — a story Leo Tolstoy later turned into the novella 'Hadji Murat'. After the Crimean War the Viceroy of the Caucasus, Prince Alexander Baryatinsky, switched to a methodical advance: clearings were cut through the forests, fortifications and roads were built, and deals were struck with communities weary of the war. In 1859 the imamate's capital, Vedeno, fell, and on August 25, 1859, Shamil, surrounded on Mount Gunib with a few hundred murids, surrendered. He and his family were settled with honor in Kaluga, allowed to go on the hajj in 1870, and he died in Medina in 1871. In the western Caucasus the war went on until 1864 and ended with the mass expulsion of the Circassians to the Ottoman Empire — hundreds of thousands of people died or became refugees.
level.shamil_1859.goal: For twenty-five years Imam Shamil leads the mountaineers' war against the empire — and surrenders only when his comrades fall away and the army methodically tightens the ring
level.shamil_1859.hint: A burned aul breeds new murids. The imam surrenders when he is left alone — and when the advance comes not in raids.
level.shamil_1859.intro: 1834. In the mountains of Dagestan and Chechnya, Imam Shamil is building an imamate — a state with sharia courts, naibs as governors and its own army. He is at war with the Russian Empire, which has been advancing into the Caucasus since 1817: under General Alexei Yermolov, fortresses were built, auls burned and the defiant deported. The war drags on for decades, both sides are cruel, and the mountain communities are split: some follow the imam, others serve the empire.
level.shamil_1859.source: Muhammad Tahir al-Qarakhi, 'The Shining of Daghestani Sabres in Certain Battles of Shamil'; Apollon Runovsky, 'Notes on Shamil' (1860)
level.shamil_1859.title: Gunib
level.shipka_1877.fact: From August 9 to 14 (August 21–26, New Style), 1877, Suleiman Pasha stormed Shipka. The defenders — about seven and a half thousand, including five Bulgarian battalions — ran out of cartridges and fought back with stones, rifle butts and even the bodies of the dead. On the critical third day of fighting, August 11 (23), the first reserves of General Fyodor Radetzky arrived, and the Turkish attacks petered out. The pass was held all autumn and through a terrible winter — during the 'Shipka vigil' thousands of soldiers froze or fell ill. Plevna fell only in December, after three bloody assaults and a siege. The war was cruel on both sides: in 1876 bashi-bazouks massacred the Bulgarian town of Batak, and in 1877–1878 tens of thousands of Muslims fled or died during the Ottoman retreat. The Treaty of San Stefano in March 1878 created a Greater Bulgaria, but the Congress of Berlin cut it down a few months later. For Bulgarians, Shipka is a place of national memory: the Freedom Monument stands on the summit.
level.shipka_1877.goal: Bulgarian volunteers and Stoletov's Russian soldiers hold the Shipka Pass against Suleiman Pasha's army until Radetzky's reserve arrives
level.shipka_1877.hint: A pass is held from the summit, not in the valley. The reserve is needed on Shipka — Plevna would swallow it.
level.shipka_1877.intro: Summer 1877. Russia is at war with the Ottoman Empire; on its side fight Bulgarian volunteers, the opalchentsi, for whom this is a war for freedom after the crushed uprising of 1876. The Russian army has crossed the Danube but has been stopped at Plevna by Osman Pasha. Only one convenient road leads across the Balkans — the Shipka Pass. It is held by General Nikolai Stoletov's small detachment, and from below comes Suleiman Pasha's army, three times stronger.
level.shipka_1877.source: Ivan Vazov, 'The Volunteers at Shipka' (1883); Preliminary Treaty of San Stefano (1878)
level.shipka_1877.title: Shipka
level.svyatoslav_965.fact: The chronicle says that Sviatoslav sent his enemies the message 'I am coming against you' and in 965 defeated the Khazars and took their fortress of Belaya Vezha — Sarkel on the Don. After that the khaganate quickly fell apart, and this shifted the balance of power in the steppe and on the trade routes — less a 'liberation of Rus'' than an opening of the steppe to new nomads. Then the prince went off to the Danube, to Bulgaria, and declared that he wished to live in Pereyaslavets: 'There is the center of my land.' In 968 the Pechenegs besieged Kyiv, where Olga was with her grandsons. In 971 Emperor John Tzimiskes besieged Sviatoslav in Dorostolon; the prince made peace and set off home. The voivode Sveneld advised going around the Dnieper rapids on horseback, but Sviatoslav went by boat; in the spring of 972 the Pecheneg prince Kurya killed him and, according to the chronicle, made a cup from his skull.
level.svyatoslav_965.goal: Sviatoslav crushes the Khazar Khaganate and goes off to fight on the Danube — but without the Khazars the steppe becomes Pecheneg, and the prince dies at the rapids
level.svyatoslav_965.hint: The fall of an old power opens the road to a new one. Whoever makes peace with the khan won't die at the rapids — but that is not how it went.
level.svyatoslav_965.intro: The 960s. Sviatoslav, son of Igor and Olga, has grown up a warrior: he sleeps on a horse blanket, carries no cooking pot and roasts his meat over the coals. East of Rus' lies the Khazar Khaganate — a realm in the steppes of the lower Volga and Don, to which the Slavs long paid tribute and with which they traded. From deep in the steppes come the nomadic Pechenegs.
level.svyatoslav_965.source: 'The Tale of Bygone Years', entries for 6472–6480 (964–972); Leo the Deacon, 'History', books VIII–IX
level.svyatoslav_965.title: Sviatoslav and Khazaria
level.tokhtamysh_1382.fact: According to the chronicle, Oleg of Ryazan showed Tokhtamysh the fords of the Oka. Dmitry Ivanovich failed to gather an army in time and left for Kostroma; Metropolitan Cyprian also abandoned the city. The defense of Moscow was led by the Lithuanian prince Ostey, a grandson of Algirdas. The Kremlin, with stone walls for the first time, beat off assaults for three days — the defenders even fired early cannons, tyufyaks, from the walls. Then the princes of Suzdal, Dmitry's brothers-in-law, came to the gates and swore that the khan would harm no one. On August 26, 1382, Ostey came out with gifts and clergy — he was killed, the gates were opened, and the city was plundered and burned. The chronicler writes of thousands dead. Moscow began paying tribute again, and Dmitry sent his son Vasily to the Horde as a hostage. This episode breaks the myth that a single battle on Kulikovo Field ended the Horde's rule.
level.tokhtamysh_1382.goal: Two years after Kulikovo, Khan Tokhtamysh suddenly appears before Moscow, burns it through deceit — and Moscow pays tribute again
level.tokhtamysh_1382.hint: The victor of Kulikovo did not sit out the siege — he left to gather an army. The city is surrendered not by the prince but by whoever believed the oath at the gates.
level.tokhtamysh_1382.intro: Summer 1382. Tokhtamysh, a descendant of Genghis Khan, has defeated Mamai and united the Horde. He demands that Moscow pay tribute as before — and suddenly sets out on campaign. Prince Oleg of Ryazan, whose land is the first in the steppe riders' path, must choose: fight or buy them off.
level.tokhtamysh_1382.source: 'The Tale of Tokhtamysh's Invasion' (Rogozhsky Chronicler, Novgorod Fourth Chronicle)
level.tokhtamysh_1382.title: Tokhtamysh's Moscow
level.tver_1327.fact: On August 15, 1327, Horde men seized a mare from the deacon Dyudko; people stood up for him and rang the bell — and the rebels wiped out the detachment and burned Chol Khan in the prince's hall. Chronicles differ on whether the prince took part. Ivan Danilovich, Prince of Moscow, nicknamed Kalita ('Moneybag'), went to the khan and came back with an army of fifty thousand under Fedorchuk: Tver, Kashin and Torzhok were ravaged, and many were taken captive. Alexander fled to Pskov. Ivan received the grand principality (at first jointly with the Prince of Suzdal, alone from 1331) and the right to collect the Horde's tribute. That is how Moscow grew: not only through 'the wisdom of its princes' but also through alliance with the khan's power. Alexander was executed in the Horde in 1339. The uprising was remembered — the song 'Shchelkan Dudentyevich' was composed about it.
level.tver_1327.goal: The people of Tver rise against the khan's envoy Chol Khan — and Ivan Kalita leads a Horde army against Tver, winning the khan's favor for it
level.tver_1327.hint: The uprising began in the street, not on the prince's orders. Executing the envoy yourself is not the same as the alarm bell. And whoever goes to repent won't be fleeing.
level.tver_1327.intro: 1327. Khan Özbeg has made Alexander Mikhailovich, Prince of Tver, Grand Prince of Vladimir — his father and brother had earlier been executed in the Horde. The khan's cousin Chol Khan, called Shchelkan in the Rus' chronicles, arrives in Tver with a large detachment. He throws the prince out of his own court, and rumors spread through the city that the envoy means to take the throne himself.
level.tver_1327.source: Rogozhsky Chronicler, entry for 1327; the Tver Collection; the song 'Shchelkan Dudentyevich'
level.tver_1327.title: The Tver Alarm Bell
level.ugra_1480.fact: Ivan III had already concluded an alliance with the Crimean Khan Mengli Giray, who struck at Podolia — and Casimir sent no help. The armies stood facing each other across the Ugra; the Horde tried to cross but was driven back with arquebuses and arrows. Ivan III summoned his son Ivan the Young to Moscow, but, according to the chronicle, the son replied: 'Better for us to die here than to go to our father.' Archbishop Vassian Rylo of Rostov, in his 'Epistle to the Ugra', reproached the grand prince for indecision. When ice bound the river, the Russian troops pulled back to Kremenets — and on November 11, 1480, Akhmat led his army away. That winter he was killed in the steppe by rivals. Later the stand on the Ugra came to be regarded as 'the end of the yoke' — a convenient simplification: dependence on the Horde had been weakening for decades, and raids and payments to steppe khans went on for a long time afterwards.
level.ugra_1480.goal: Khan Akhmat marches on Moscow, but his ally never comes, and Ivan III's son holds the crossings — and the Horde leaves without a battle
level.ugra_1480.hint: This war was won without a great battle: through alliances and stubbornness at the fords. A son who obeyed his father's order would no longer hold the fords.
level.ugra_1480.intro: Autumn 1480. For several years Ivan III has paid no tribute to the Great Horde. Khan Akhmat leads his army to the border, counting on an alliance with Casimir IV, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania. Moscow is in turmoil: the grand prince wavers, and his wife Sophia Palaiologina, niece of the last Byzantine emperor, leaves for the north with the treasury.
level.ugra_1480.source: Vologda-Perm Chronicle; Vassian Rylo, 'Epistle to the Ugra' (1480)
level.ugra_1480.title: The Great Stand on the Ugra
level.valuev_1863.fact: In January 1863 an uprising broke out in the Kingdom of Poland. Part of the press and officialdom, including the publicist Mikhail Katkov, began to portray the Ukrainian movement as a Polish intrigue against Russia. On July 18, 1863, the Minister of the Interior, Pyotr Valuev, sent the censors a secret circular: educational and religious books and books for popular reading in the 'Little Russian dialect' were not to be passed, with only 'belles-lettres' permitted.
