The circular repeated the claim that 'there has been no separate Little Russian language, there is none, and there can be none' — this was the position of the movement's opponents, not a scholarly fact: the Ukrainian language existed and was written and printed long before 1863. Kostomarov argued with the authorities in letters and in print, but the ban stayed. 'Osnova' had already closed by then, and the Sunday schools were shut down. In 1876 the Ems Decree tightened the restrictions; they were eased only after the revolution of 1905.
level.valuev_1863.goal: Ukrainian primers and journals frighten the authorities after the Polish uprising — and Minister Valuev issues a secret circular banning educational and religious books in Ukrainian
level.valuev_1863.hint: What gets banned is what has already appeared. It is not the book that frightens the minister but the uprising next door. If the historian manages to change his mind, there will be no ban.
level.valuev_1863.intro: 1861. After the abolition of serfdom, the journal 'Osnova', edited by Vasyl Bilozersky, appears in Petersburg; among its main authors are the historian Nikolai Kostomarov and the writer Panteleimon Kulish. The Ukrainian language is alive in literature too: Ivan Kotliarevsky's 'Eneida' came out as early as 1798, and Taras Shevchenko's 'Kobzar' in 1840. Enthusiasts open Sunday schools and print primers, and Pylyp Morachevsky's Ukrainian translation of the Gospels is submitted to the censors.
level.valuev_1863.source: Circular of the Minister of the Interior P. A. Valuev (July 18, 1863); Nikolai Kostomarov, 'Autobiography'
level.valuev_1863.title: The Valuev Circular
level.war_1914.fact: On July 29 Nicholas II signed the decree on general mobilization, but in the evening, after a telegram from 'Willy', he replaced it with a partial one. On July 30 Sazonov and the generals persuaded him to restore general mobilization. Germany demanded that it be canceled, and on August 1, 1914, declared war on Russia. The causes of the world war were many, and no single power was its sole culprit or sole victim. The first months brought the catastrophe of Samsonov's army in East Prussia, 1915 the Great Retreat from Poland and Lithuania. In June 1916 General Alexei Brusilov struck the Austrians not in one place but along the whole front at once, and the breakthrough threw them back dozens of kilometers; Austria-Hungary lost about a million men, prisoners included, but Russian losses were enormous too. The war, millions of dead and hunger in the cities led to the revolution of 1917.
level.war_1914.goal: Sazonov persuades the Tsar to order general mobilization, Germany answers with war — and two years later Brusilov breaks through the Austrian front
level.war_1914.hint: The cousins' telegrams only slow the machinery down. Brusilov does not strike with a fist at a single point.
level.war_1914.intro: July 1914. Austria-Hungary has presented Serbia with an ultimatum after the archduke's assassination in Sarajevo. Russia regards itself as Serbia's protector and is bound by alliance to France. Foreign Minister Sergei Sazonov is pressing Nicholas II to mobilize: the vast empire needs weeks to assemble its army. Meanwhile Kaiser Wilhelm II — the Empress's first cousin — sends 'Nicky' telegrams begging him to stop.
level.war_1914.source: Correspondence of Wilhelm II and Nicholas II (July 1914); A. A. Brusilov, 'My Memoirs' (1929)
level.war_1914.title: The Great War
level.yarlyk_1252.fact: The chronicle reports briefly: Alexander went to Sartaq, and 'Nevryuy's host' came against Andrey. Near Pereslavl-Zalessky Andrey's army was defeated; he himself fled to Novgorod and from there to Sweden; 'a countless multitude' of people from the ravaged lands were led into captivity. Alexander returned from the Horde with the yarlyk for the Grand Principality of Vladimir. Whether he complained to the khan about his brother, the sources do not say — later historians argue about it. The 'Life' portrays Alexander as a defender against the West; the chronicles also show a politician who built his power within the Horde's system: he helped carry out the Horde census of 1257–1259 and put down revolts against the tribute collectors. Andrey later returned and was reconciled with his brother.
level.yarlyk_1252.goal: Alexander Nevsky rides to the Horde, Nevryuy's army crushes his brother Andrey — and Alexander receives the yarlyk for Vladimir
level.yarlyk_1252.hint: A grand prince is made by the yarlyk, not by the sword. Whoever rises against the Horde together with his brother won't receive the yarlyk.
level.yarlyk_1252.intro: 1252. The throne of Vladimir is held, by a yarlyk from distant Karakorum, by the younger brother — Andrey Yaroslavich; the elder, Alexander, has been given ravaged Kyiv and Novgorod. Andrey is married to the daughter of Daniel, Prince of Galicia, who is seeking allies against the Horde. Alexander rides to the Horde — to Batu's son Sartaq.
level.yarlyk_1252.source: Laurentian Chronicle, entry for 1252; 'The Life of Alexander Nevsky'
level.yarlyk_1252.title: The Yarlyk and Nevryuy's Host
level.yaroslav_1015.fact: The chronicle and 'The Tale of Boris and Gleb' relate that the druzhina urged Boris to take the throne of Kyiv, but he answered that he would not raise his hand against his elder brother; Sviatopolk's men killed him on the Alta River, and then the young Gleb as well. The Church venerates them as the first Rus' saints — martyrs who chose not to resist. In 1016 Yaroslav, with Novgorodians and Varangians, defeated Sviatopolk near Liubech; Sviatopolk returned in 1018 with his father-in-law, the Polish King Bolesław the Brave, and in 1019 was finally defeated on the Alta and fled. Yaroslav, called the Wise, ruled Kyiv until 1054: under him the 'Russkaya Pravda' was compiled and St. Sophia's Cathedral was built. The chronicle's moral is simpler than the politics: on the basis of the Scandinavian 'Eymundar þáttr', some historians allow that Boris may have been killed not by Sviatopolk but by Yaroslav's mercenaries. The question is disputed.
level.yaroslav_1015.goal: After Vladimir's death Sviatopolk kills his brothers Boris and Gleb, and Yaroslav, with Novgorodians and Varangians, takes revenge and sits on the throne of Kyiv
level.yaroslav_1015.hint: There will be no martyr if he marches on Kyiv himself. The avenger needs an army — and an enemy everyone considers accursed.
level.yaroslav_1015.intro: Summer 1015. Prince Vladimir, who baptized Rus', is dying. He has many sons by different wives, and the order of succession is unclear. In Kyiv the eldest, Sviatopolk, seizes power. Vladimir's favorite son Boris is returning from a campaign against the Pechenegs with his father's druzhina. Yaroslav sits in Novgorod and has already managed to quarrel with his father.
level.yaroslav_1015.source: 'The Tale of Bygone Years', entries for 6523–6527 (1015–1019); 'The Tale of Boris and Gleb' (11th century); 'Eymundar þáttr'
level.yaroslav_1015.title: The Brothers After Vladimir
